title: how are black holes formed
description: explain on a highschool level the physics of how black holes are formed

script.draft:
# HOW ARE BLACK HOLES FORMED

---

[VISUAL: a massive glowing star filling the frame, pulsing with light and heat, digital art style]
Imagine something so dense that nothing — not even light — can escape its gravity. That's a black hole. And one of the wildest things about them? They start as something we can actually see. A star.

Stars like our Sun are basically a constant tug-of-war. Gravity pulls inward. Nuclear fusion pushes outward. For millions — sometimes billions — of years, those two forces stay balanced.

---

[VISUAL: cross-section of a star showing its iron core glowing at the center, surrounded by layers of lighter elements]
But massive stars — we're talking at least eight times bigger than our Sun — eventually run into a problem. They burn through their fuel, layer by layer, until they're left with an iron core. And here's the thing about iron: you can't fuse it to release energy. The fusion just... stops.

When that happens, the outward push disappears. Gravity wins — instantly.

The core collapses in less than a second. The outer layers come crashing inward at roughly a quarter the speed of light, then rebound outward in a catastrophic explosion called a supernova.

---

[VISUAL: dramatic supernova explosion radiating outward in deep space, bright shockwave against a star field]
A supernova is one of the most powerful events in the universe. But what's left behind is even more extreme. If the remaining core is massive enough — more than about three times the mass of our Sun — gravity doesn't stop. It keeps collapsing. Forever.

The core crushes down into an infinitely small point called a singularity. And surrounding it, a boundary forms — the event horizon. Cross that line, and there's no coming back.

---

[VISUAL: artistic rendering of a black hole with an accretion disk glowing orange and white, deep space background]
That's a black hole. Not a hole in space — a region where gravity is so extreme that space itself curves closed around it.

And right now, there's a supermassive one sitting at the center of our own galaxy, four million times the mass of our Sun.

It's not coming for us. But it's definitely there.
